questions.question: What does successful GraphQL schema validation prove?
options: The operation is cheap and the caller may read every field
The document is structurally valid for the schema, but cost and authorization still need separate checks
Every resolver dependency is available
The response cannot contain execution errors
questions.explanation: Validation checks the operation against the type system. Demand control, authentication, domain authorization, dependency health, and execution correctness are separate boundaries.

questions.question: An operation has a fixed cost of 12 points and requests 20 items at 5 points each. What is its modeled cost?
questions.explanation: The model is fixed cost plus list size times per-item cost: 12 + (20 x 5) = 112 points.

questions.question: Why is a depth limit alone insufficient demand control?
options: GraphQL operations never contain nested fields
A shallow operation can still use many aliases, broad fields, large lists, or expensive resolvers
Depth limits apply only to mutations
A depth limit automatically batches backend access
questions.explanation: Depth captures only one dimension. Breadth, aliases, batch size, list cardinality, field weights, and client traffic can create high work without deep nesting.

questions.question: What is the safest normal lifetime for a DataLoader-style memoization cache?
options: The lifetime of the whole server process for every user
One GraphQL request and its authorization context
Until the database is restarted
Exactly one resolver function call
questions.explanation: Request-scoped loaders batch sibling resolver work and deduplicate repeated keys without leaking values across users, permissions, locales, or transactions.

questions.question: A nullable reviewSummary resolver fails while required product fields succeed. What can a conforming execution result contain?
options: No data under any circumstance
Product data with reviewSummary set to null plus an execution error path
Only an HTTP redirect
A successful reviewSummary copied from another user
questions.explanation: A field execution error is represented as null at that response position and included in errors. Because the field is nullable, sibling product data can remain.

questions.question: What happens when a failed field is declared non-null?
options: GraphQL silently replaces it with an empty string
The null propagates to the nearest nullable parent and may remove a larger subtree
The server retries every mutation automatically
The schema is rewritten to make the field nullable
questions.explanation: Non-null value completion cannot place null at that response position, so the error propagates through non-null parents until a nullable boundary can contain it.

questions.question: A mutation times out after calling a payment service. Which design best handles a client retry?
options: Trust top-level mutation serialization to prevent a second charge
Use a stable idempotency key and reconcile the payment outcome before repeating the side effect
Make every mutation field nullable
Disable operation naming
questions.explanation: Serial execution orders top-level mutation fields within one operation; it does not deduplicate later requests or coordinate an ambiguous external effect. Idempotency and reconciliation do.
